items.prose: £5,000.00 is invested at 3% a year, compounded yearly, for 6 years.
items.question: What is it worth after 6 years?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by 1.03 once for each of the 6 years.

byKey.simple: £5,900.00 adds 3% of £5,000.00 six times: simple interest. Each year's 3% is on a larger balance.
byKey.interest: That is the interest alone. Add the £5,000.00 invested.

explain.text: Six years multiply by $1.03^6 = 1.194052$. So £5,000.00 becomes £5,970.26. Simple interest would give £5,900.00; the extra £70.26 is interest on interest.

items.prose: A payment of £2,500.00 is due in 4 years. The rate is 6% a year, compounded.
items.question: What is it worth today?

byKey.simple: You divided by $1 + 0.06 \times 4 = 1.24$. Four compounded years back divide by $1.06^4 = 1.2625$.
byKey.once: You discounted for one year. The payment is four years away.

explain.text: Four years back divide by $1.06^4 = 1.262477$. So £2,500.00 in 4 years is worth £1,980.23 today. Check: $1980.23 \times 1.262477 = 2500.00$.

items.prose: A loan charges 9% a year nominal, compounded monthly.
items.question: What is its effective annual rate? Give a percentage to two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compound $1 + \tfrac{0.09}{12}$ over 12 months, then take away 1.

byKey.nominal: 9% is the nominal rate. Monthly compounding charges interest on interest within the year.
byKey.month: 0.75% is one month's charge. The effective rate covers the year.

explain.text: Each month charges $0.09/12 = 0.0075$. Twelve months give $1.0075^{12} = 1.0938$. So the loan costs 9.38% effective.

items.prose: A project costs £800.00 today and pays £300.00 at the end of each of the next 3 years. The rate is 6%.
items.question: What is its NPV?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount each £300.00, add them, then take away £800.00.

byKey.undisc: You added the cash without discounting. Each £300.00 is worth less the later it comes.
byKey.no-cost: That is the value of the payments. Take away the £800.00 cost.

explain.text: The three payments are worth £283.02, £267.00 and £251.89 today, £801.90 in all. Take away £800.00: NPV £1.90. The IRR is just above 6%.

items.prose: An index fund is expected to grow 6% a year, compounded.
items.question: Which is the best estimate of how long it takes to double?

options.why: That is simple growth, $100 \div 6$. Compounding doubles sooner.
You read the rate as the doubling time. Divide 72 by 6.
Doubling at 6% a year takes much longer. Divide 72 by 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the rule of 72.

explain.text: The rule of 72 gives $72 \div 6 = 12$ years. Exactly, $\ln 2 / \ln 1.06 = 11.90$ years. Simple growth would take 16.7 years.

items.prose: £10,000.00 is due in 2 years. The discount rate is 6% a year nominal, compounded monthly.
items.question: What is it worth today?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount by $1.005$ for each of the 24 months.

byKey.annual: You discounted at 6% compounded yearly. Monthly compounding means 24 steps of $1.005$.
byKey.simple: You divided by $1 + 0.06 \times 2 = 1.12$, simple interest. Compound back over 24 months.

explain.text: Each month back divides by $1 + \tfrac{0.06}{12} = 1.005$, and there are 24 months. So $10000 / 1.005^{24} = 8871.86$. The effective rate is 6.17%, so it is worth less than at 6% annual.

items.prose: A fund targets 8% a year effective. Its manager wants the matching quarterly return.
items.question: What quarterly return compounds to 8% a year? Give a percentage to two decimal places.

byKey.div: You divided 8% by 4. Four quarters of 2% compound to 8.24%, too much.

explain.text: We need $(1 + x)^4 = 1.08$, so $x = 1.08^{1/4} - 1 = 0.0194$. Dividing by 4 gives 2%, which compounds to 8.24%. Effective rates convert by roots, not by division.

items.prose: Projects A and B each cost £2,000.00. A pays £2,600.00 in year 2. B pays £1,300.00 in year 1 and £1,200.00 in year 2.
items.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: A has the higher NPV at 5%, B at 10%
A wins at both rates, because it pays £100.00 more in total
options.why: At 10%, A's NPV is £148.76 and B's £173.55. A's cash comes later, so a high rate hurts it more.

options.text: B wins at both rates, because it pays sooner
options.why: At 5%, A's NPV is £358.28 and B's £326.53. At low rates the larger total wins.

options.text: They rank the same at every rate
options.why: The ranking flips near 7.7%, where the two NPVs are equal.

feedback.correct: A wins at 5%, B at 10%: the ranking flips near 7.7%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out both NPVs at 5% and at 10%.

explain.text: At 5%: A £358.28, B £326.53. At 10%: A £148.76, B £173.55. The NPVs are equal at about 7.7%, so the rate decides the ranking.

items.prose: A preference share pays £45.00 at the end of every year, for ever. Investors want 3% a year.
items.question: What is it worth today?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A perpetuity is worth $C/r$.

byKey.pct: You divided by 3, not 0.03. The rate goes in as a decimal.
byKey.due: That adds a payment today. The first is a year away.

explain.text: A payment for ever is a perpetuity, worth $C/r = 45/0.03 = 1500$. Each year's £45.00 is exactly 3% of £1,500.00. If investors wanted 4%, it would be worth £1,125.00.
